strengths: The core idea—performing DDIM/PF-ODE inversion to map an input into the final latent xT and scoring via prior likelihood—is clean, well-motivated, and provides a sensible theoretical bridge between diffusion-based and flow-based anomaly detection (Sec. 4.2, Eq. 16). Removing the need to tune the diffusion/perturbation strength addresses a genuine, widely acknowledged weakness of reconstruction-based diffusion AD methods.

The paper is unusually honest about a counterintuitive failure mode: the 'reverse-scoring' phenomenon (Sec. 5.4, Fig. 2), where increasing S degrades NLL-based detection, and connects it to known OOD/likelihood pathologies in flow-based models [19, 20]. This analysis is a genuine contribution beyond the method itself.

The ablation in Table 4 is informative: it compares reconstruction-based vs. inversion-based use of the same diffusion model across steps S and perturbation levels, empirically supporting the claim that inversion is more robust to hyperparameter choices.

Inference cost is a clear practical win: 2–5 NFEs and ~64 ms latency vs. hundreds of NFEs and seconds for GLAD/AnoDDPM/DDAD (Tables 1–3), and the evaluation covers both MVTecAD and VisA with image- and pixel-level metrics.
The proposed method avoids synthetic/pseudo anomalies, keeping it within the strict unsupervised setting—contrast with DAD, which achieves comparable speed only via pseudo-anomalies.
weaknesses: Detection accuracy is not state-of-the-art and the paper overstates its results. On MVTecAD the average is (97.3, 93.7) for Ours and (99.1, 94.8) for Ours*, clearly below DAD (99.7, 98.7), DDAD (99.8, 98.1), and GLAD (99.3, 98.6), particularly at the pixel level (94.8 vs. 98.7). On VisA the gap is severe: 79.1/87.4 (Ours) vs. ~98.5/98.6 for GLAD/DDAD. The abstract's 'new state-of-the-art speed-AUC trade-off' claim needs to be far more carefully qualified; no precision-recall or latency-accuracy curves are provided to substantiate a Pareto-dominance claim.

The claimed speed-AUC superiority ignores strong non-diffusion baselines. Memory-bank methods (PatchCore, PaDiM, etc.) achieve ~99%+ image-level AUC on MVTecAD at millisecond latencies (EfficienAD, cited as [1], is explicitly a millisecond-level method). Restricting the latency comparison to diffusion-based methods undermines the headline contribution.

The final anomaly score is an ad hoc heuristic: a sum of a normalized channel-norm map and the normalized max–min difference of spatial norms (Eq. 17, Algorithm 1). The paper concedes that plain prior log-likelihood fails (reverse-scoring) and patches it with this heuristic, but provides no theoretical justification and limited ablation of alternative spatial scores. The 'Ours*' variant additionally tunes S in {2,...,5}, which partially contradicts the 'no tuning required' narrative.

Serious writing/polish problems: Section 3.4 contains two nearly verbatim duplicated paragraphs, and Section 4.3 contains a duplicated block describing the feature-space diffusion model twice. This suggests the manuscript was not carefully prepared and undermines confidence in overall rigor.

Notational and algorithmic ambiguities hinder reproducibility: Algorithm 1 uses indices τ_i without defining τ_0 (presumably the feature z itself), the scoring lines mix x, x_norm, and normalization functions without precise definitions, and no code release is mentioned. Hyperparameter details beyond backbone/optimizer (e.g., UNet capacity, image resolution, feature channel settings per dataset) are incomplete.

The omission of the Jacobian term in Eq. (16) is justified only empirically and by appeal to flow-based practice; a more careful analysis of when this approximation is valid (e.g., dependence on S and the discretization error of the Euler inversion) would strengthen the contribution. The theoretical connection claimed in Sec. 4.1 (point 3) remains shallow.

Some per-category results are weak and unexplained (e.g., metal nut at (93.6, 71.9) and screw at 88.7 image-AUC on MVTecAD; macaroni2 at 47.9 on VisA), and the paper offers no analysis of failure cases, which limits insight into when the prior-likelihood assumption breaks down.

strengths: The core idea is simple and appealing: instead of the reconstruct-and-compare paradigm, the method inverts the input along the PF-ODE and scores typicality of the final latent, removing the need to tune the perturbation timestep and reducing NFE to 2-5, which yields a genuine inference-speed improvement (64 ms vs. 617-11950 ms for competing diffusion methods in Table 1).

The paper includes an honest and informative ablation (Table 4) comparing reconstruction-based and inversion-based use of the *same* trained diffusion model across varying step counts and perturbation strengths, isolating the benefit of the inversion formulation.

The empirical investigation of the 'reverse-scoring' phenomenon (Sec. 5.4, Fig. 2), where NLL-based scores degrade with more diffusion steps, connects the observations to the known 'typicality' pathology in flow-based OOD detection literature and is a useful analysis for the community.
The method avoids pseudo-anomaly generation, placing it in a stricter unsupervised setting than several competitors (e.g., DAD, GLAD), and the authors flag this distinction explicitly.
weaknesses: Detection accuracy is substantially below the state of the art, undermining the headline claims. On MVTecAD the average image-level AUC is 97.3 (Ours) / 99.1 (Ours*) vs. 99.8 (DDAD) and 99.7 (DAD); pixel-level AUC drops to 93.7/94.8 vs. ~98.3-98.7. On VisA the gap is severe: 79.1 (Ours) / 95.8 (Ours*) vs. 98.9 (DDAD) and 99.5 (GLAD), with outright failures (macaroni2: 47.9 image AUC; capsules: 58.3). The abstract's 'new state-of-the-art speed-AUC trade-off' is therefore true only on the speed axis; the paper is effectively a fast but considerably less accurate detector.

The comparison set is restricted to diffusion-based methods, so the speed-AUC trade-off claim ignores non-diffusion baselines. In particular EfficientAD [1], cited by the authors, reports ~99.1 image-level AUC on MVTecAD at millisecond-level latency—strictly better than the proposed method on both axes. Claiming a SOTA trade-off while omitting this direct competitor is a material overstatement.

There is an internal contradiction in the experimental protocol: the paper criticizes prior work for hyperparameter tuning that 'implicitly exploits anomaly information', yet 'Ours*' tunes S per category over {2,3,4,5}, and best-performing checkpoints are selected (Sec. 5.2). The abstract's 0.991 AUC and 15 FPS figures correspond to this tuned variant, while the untuned setting is 97.3 AUC—the headline result conflates the two.

The final anomaly score is a heuristic composition (Algorithm 1): a sum of two independently normalized terms, ||x_T||_2 and the max-min range of the spatial norm map. There is no principled justification for this combination, no sensitivity analysis of the normalization scheme, and the theoretically motivated NLL score actually fails (reverse scoring). The paper acknowledges this is an open question but the presented detector rests on an ad hoc fix.

Severe writing-quality problems indicate a lack of polish: Section 4.3 contains a nearly verbatim duplicated block (two consecutive paragraphs describing the feature-space diffusion model), and Section 3.4 repeats the same sentences about NFE, pseudo-anomalies, and Table 1 twice. Fig. 2 shows score histograms for only a single category (hazelnut), which is not enough to substantiate the reverse-scoring analysis broadly.

The novelty is modest: DDIM inversion plus latent-density scoring is close to ScoreDD [29] (PF-ODE-based, 15 NFE) and to flow-based density anomaly detection; the main deltas are few-step inversion and the heuristic spatial-norm score. The Jacobian term in Eq. (16) is dropped with only an empirical justification, and the theoretical connection claimed as a contribution (point 3 of the advantage list) is not developed.

Evaluation breadth is narrow: only MVTecAD and VisA, no results on other benchmarks (e.g., BTAD, real-IAD), no standard-deviation/multiple-run reporting despite from-scratch training of a diffusion model per category, and no mention of code release, limiting reproducibility.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: instead of the noisy-then-denoise reconstruction loop, the method runs DDIM/PF-ODE inversion forward to x_T and scores typicality of the latent under the Gaussian prior. This removes the noise-strength/perturbation-timestep hyperparameter that plagues reconstruction-based diffusion AD, and reduces NFE to 2-5, which is a meaningful and practical contribution.

The comparison in Table 1 is a useful contribution in itself, systematically characterizing prior diffusion-based AD methods along syn-anomaly usage, NFE, latency, timestep tuning, sampler, and score type; it clearly positions the proposed approach.

The ablation in Table 4 directly addresses the central design question (reconstruction vs. inversion) using the same trained diffusion model, and the inversion approach is consistently stronger and insensitive to the denoising start point. The analysis of the 'reverse-scoring' phenomenon (Fig. 2), connecting it to known likelihood-pathology results in OOD detection [19, 20], is an interesting and honest empirical finding.

The method requires no synthetic/pseudo anomalies (unlike DAD, GLAD, TransFusion, DiffAD), which is a real advantage for strict unsupervised anomaly detection, and the very low latency (64 ms) is a substantial engineering win.
Experiments cover both MVTecAD and VisA with image- and pixel-level metrics, and include comparison against a reasonably broad set of recent diffusion-based competitors.
weaknesses: Detection accuracy lags the state of the art substantially in several places, weakening the headline claim. On MVTecAD, 'Ours' achieves only (97.3, 93.7) average AUC vs. DAD (99.7, 98.7) and DDAD (99.8, 98.1); pixel-level performance is notably worse (93.7 vs. ~98). On VisA the gap is large: 'Ours' averages (79.1, 87.4) vs. ~99 for baselines, with individual categories as low as 47.9 and 58.3 image-level AUC. The abstract's claim of a 'new state-of-the-art speed-AUC trade-off' is only defensible if one weights speed very heavily; the paper should state this trade-off more carefully.

The claimed advantage of 'no tuning' is partially contradicted by the evaluation protocol: 'Ours*' tunes S in {2,3,4,5}, and the authors report results 'based on the best-performing checkpoints' (Sec. 5.2), which risks test-set selection. Only the fixed S=2 result is tuning-free, and that is the weakest variant. This inconsistency between the method's main selling point and the reported numbers needs clarification.

The image-level anomaly score (difference between max and min of the per-pixel latent norms, plus normalization steps in Algorithm 1) is an ad hoc heuristic introduced to patch the reverse-scoring problem, without theoretical justification. The paper itself concedes that 'a rigorous theoretical interpretation ... remain[s] open questions.' The exact composition in Algorithm 1 (Normalize applied to a scalar?) is also under-specified.

Novelty relative to ScoreDD [29], which already uses PF-ODE trajectories for diffusion-based anomaly detection at 15 NFE, is not clearly delineated. The differences (latent density vs. score norm, feature-space diffusion) are meaningful but incremental, and the related-work discussion does not articulate why the proposed scoring is preferable.

Significant presentation flaws: Section 3.4 contains two nearly verbatim duplicated paragraphs, and Section 4.3 repeats the same paragraph twice (page 5), suggesting the paper was not carefully proofread. Notation is inconsistent (feature extraction defines z = g_phi(x) but Algorithm 1 and Section 4.4 operate on x), 'asinversion' appears as a typo, and the hardware used for latency measurement is never specified, making the speed claims hard to verify.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, several hyperparameters (backbone feature choice, image resolution, diffusion model size) are only partially specified, and Table 3 has many missing baseline entries that make cross-method comparison on VisA incomplete.

Table 4 shows inversion (NLL) performance degrades sharply with more steps (96.9 at S=3 down to 59.5 at S=1000), and the proposed spatial-norm fix, while effective, is only empirically validated; the mechanism behind why short partial inversion suffices (and when it would fail) deserves deeper analysis.

strengths: The proposed 'detection via noising in latent space' paradigm is a clean and well-motivated reframing of diffusion-based AD: instead of perturb-and-denoise with tuned noise strength, InvAD traces the PF-ODE via DDIM inversion to a final latent and scores typicality under the tractable prior, which provably removes the timestep-tuning hyperparameter that plagues reconstruction-based diffusion AD.

The efficiency claim is well supported: with only S=3 NFEs the method reaches 88.1 FPS on MVTecAD, roughly 2.2x faster than OmiAD (39.4 FPS) and one to two orders of magnitude faster than GLAD, DDAD, DiAD, etc., without requiring distillation training (Table 1, Table 2).

Evaluation breadth is strong for the area: three industrial benchmarks (MVTecAD, VisA, MPDD) in both multi-class and single-class settings (Tables 2, 3, 11), a medical benchmark (BMAD, Table 12), and plug-and-play integration into two other diffusion AD frameworks (DeCoDiff, MDM in Table 5), which supports the model-agnostic inference-stage claim.

Informative ablations: the inversion-vs-reconstruction comparison in Table 4 convincingly demonstrates the fragility of noise-strength/timestep tuning in the reconstruction paradigm while the inversion variant is stable at small S; Table 13 shows the NLL+Abs scoring combination is what makes robustness to S possible; backbone and diffusion-architecture ablations (Tables 6, 7) are useful for practitioners.

The supplementary material is substantive: full DDIM-inversion derivation (Sec. E/F), dataset statistics, hyperparameters, hardware details, and fixed seeds, which supports reproducibility (code link pending but the described setup is detailed).
weaknesses: The 'state-of-the-art' claim is overstated. On MVTecAD multi-class, OmiAD achieves higher mAD (85.3 vs 83.7), higher pixel AU-ROC (97.7 vs 97.5), notably higher pixel AP (52.6 vs 46.5), and higher AU-PRO (93.2 vs 92.7). InvAD wins mainly on image-level metrics and speed; the paper should frame this as a favorable efficiency-accuracy trade-off rather than overall SOTA.

In single-class results (Tables 3, 11), InvAD is clearly not the best: DDAD averages (99.8, 98.7) vs InvAD (99.1, 97.3) on MVTecAD, and pixel-level AU-ROC is below DAD, GLAD, and DDAD on many categories (e.g., tile 94.4, wood 92.3). The text's 'consistently improves efficiency with competitive accuracy' is accurate but the framing in the abstract/introduction inflates the positioning.

The plug-and-play result cuts both ways: on DeCoDiff, InvAD reduces image AU-ROC by 2.0-2.8 points on both datasets (Table 5). 'Minor sacrifice' understates a nontrivial accuracy regression for one of the two tested frameworks, weakening the model-agnostic claim.

The core mechanism is empirically but not analytically grounded. It is counterintuitive that more accurate inversion (larger S) degrades performance (99.0 at S=3 to 95.4 at S=1000 in Table 4; same trend for the Abs score in Table 13), yet no theoretical account is given for why coarse Euler inversion helps AD or why the heuristic score abs(max-min)+sum of per-pixel norms is appropriate. A clearer explanation of the failure mode at large S would strengthen the contribution.

The anomaly scoring is quite heuristic (norm map, max-min difference, upsampling from h×w to H×W), and localization quality correspondingly lags reconstruction-based competitors; the pixel-level gap suggests the method is better suited to detection than localization, which should be discussed explicitly.

Practical cost is under-discussed: the primary configuration is a ~1.2B-parameter DiT-gigant trained 300 epochs on 8xH200 GPUs, which is a heavy training budget for industrial AD; efficiency is reported only at inference. Also, FPS comparisons use batch-size 64 with adjustments for small test sets, and cross-method FPS comparability (different resolutions/backbones) deserves more care.

Presentation issues that should be fixed: inconsistency between 'three' datasets (abstract) and 'four' benchmarks (introduction); garbled Figure 1 caption ('paradigm. and Conventional...'); typos ('acclerate', 'compuatation', 'image-lavel'); the FastFlow citation (Um et al., PVLDB 2023) points to an unrelated systems paper rather than the FastFlow AD method; and the vague 'Project —' / 'Code —' placeholders suggest the code release is not yet verifiable.

Relative novelty is moderate: scoring by score-norm/typicality for OOD detection closely follows Heng et al. (2024), and DDIM inversion is standard; the contribution is their adaptation to latent-feature diffusion AD rather than a fundamentally new technique.

strengths: The paper proposes a genuinely interesting reframing of diffusion-based anomaly detection: instead of perturb-then-reconstruct, it inverts the input to the noise latent via the PF-ODE and scores typicality of the inverted latent. This eliminates noise-strength tuning and achieves a large inference speedup (88 FPS vs. ~0.2–17 FPS for prior diffusion methods in Tables 1 and 3) without requiring distillation.

The experimental coverage is broad and mostly thorough: three industrial benchmarks (MVTecAD, VisA, MPDD) in both multi-class and single-class settings, a medical benchmark (BMAD), a plug-and-play evaluation on DeCoDiff and MDM (Table 5), and ablations on feature encoders, diffusion architectures, scoring schemes, and the number of inversion steps.

The step-budget comparison in Table 4 is a useful analysis showing that reconstruction-based accuracy is highly sensitive to the perturbation ratio while the proposed inversion approach performs best with very few steps (S=3, 99.0 AU-ROC), directly supporting the claimed tuning-free advantage.

The supplementary material provides a complete derivation of the DDIM inversion used, detailed hyperparameters, hardware specifications, and additional per-category results, which supports reproducibility of the reported pipeline.

The manuscript is technically sound in its formulation: the Euler-discretized inversion (Eqs. 6–7) follows correctly from the PF-ODE of DDIM, and the claimed one-to-one mapping between normal data and the prior is consistent with deterministic ODE behavior.
weaknesses: Novelty is more incremental than the 'new paradigm' framing suggests. Typicality/norm-based scoring of inverted or score-space quantities already exists: ScoreDD (Teng et al. 2023) uses ||∇x p_θ(x_t)||_2, and Heng et al. (2024) — which the authors explicitly cite as inspiration — measures the score-norm as an OOD typicality proxy. The main contribution is applying this idea in a latent feature space with few-step inversion for industrial AD, which is an application-level combination rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The most discriminative baseline question is not addressed: because the method operates on frozen EfficientNet-B4 features and Table 6 shows performance is dominated by the encoder choice (87.1 with VAE → 99.0 with EfficientNet), a simple non-diffusion feature baseline with the same backbone (e.g., PatchCore-style kNN distance or Mahalanobis/norm scoring on EfficientNet-B4 features) would very likely be fast and competitive. Without this control, the paper cannot demonstrate that the diffusion inversion machinery — 1223M parameters trained for 300 epochs on 8×H200 — is actually necessary versus the pretrained features doing the work.

Image-level accuracy gains over the strongest recent competitor are marginal (MVTecAD 99.0 vs. 98.8; VisA 96.9 vs. 95.3; MPDD 96.5 vs. 93.7 for OmiAD), and pixel-level results are actually worse on MVTecAD (pixel AP 46.5 vs. 52.6; AU-PRO 92.7 vs. 93.2). Given this, the headline contribution is efficiency, but the efficiency comparison is confounded: FPS numbers compare methods with very different backbones, resolutions, and model sizes, and OmiAD already uses only 1 NFE.

The counterintuitive behavior in Table 4 — inversion performance degrading monotonically as more accurate inversion is used (99.0 at S=3 down to 95.4 at S=1000) — is never explained. Under the paper's own theoretical framing, exact inversion should best expose the density gap between normal and anomalous latents, so this trend suggests the method may exploit coarse-inversion artifacts rather than principled typicality, undermining the motivation.

The anomaly scoring is largely ad hoc. The image score s = |max(A) − min(A)| + Σ A[u,v] (Algorithm 1) is heuristic, the combination rule between NLL and the Abs term is not specified (only aggregate results in supplementary Table 13), and no theoretical or ablation-based justification is given for why the max–min spread of per-pixel channel norms of z_T should be anomaly-discriminative. The pixel map is also only an upsampled h×w feature-norm map, which limits localization fidelity.

The plug-and-play claim is weakened by the DeCoDiff result in Table 5: accuracy drops by 2.0 and 2.8 AU-ROC points on MVTecAD and VisA (99.3→97.0, 96.1→93.2), which the text characterizes as 'minor sacrifice' but is substantial in this field. The method is thus model-agnostic only in a qualified sense.

Per-category results reveal brittleness: e.g., macaroni2 at 86.9 image AU-ROC on VisA (vs. 99.9 for GLAD) and capsules at 92.1, with no failure analysis of when and why inversion-based typicality fails.

Presentation is rough for a submission at this level: numerous typos ('denosing', 'acclerate', 'compuatation', 'image-lavel', 'uncertainly'), a garbled Figure 1 caption ('paradigm. and Conventional'), a duplicated 'Equation Equation (21)', and an inconsistency between the abstract ('three widely used image AD datasets') and the text ('four widely-used AD benchmarks'). No variance, confidence intervals, or significance testing is reported anywhere, and the Project/Code fields are empty, further weakening reproducibility despite the detailed supplement.

strengths: The paper clearly articulates a new framing for diffusion-based anomaly detection ('detection via noising in latent space') that sidesteps the well-known noise-strength tuning and multi-step denoising issues of reconstruction-based diffusion AD methods; the motivation (Table 1) is well grounded in a systematic comparison of prior methods.

The efficiency results are convincing and substantial: ~2x+ speedup over the fastest prior diffusion AD method (88.1 vs 39.4 FPS on MVTecAD) with only 3 NFEs, without requiring distillation, while maintaining strong image-level accuracy (99.0 AU-ROC on MVTecAD multi-class; best image-level results on VisA and MPDD).

The evaluation is broad and thorough: three industrial benchmarks in multi-class and single-class settings, a medical benchmark (BMAD) in the supplement, per-category results, a plug-and-play generalizability study on DeCoDiff and MDM (Table 5), and multiple ablations covering the scoring scheme (Table 13), feature encoders (Table 6), diffusion architectures (Table 7), and the inversion-vs-reconstruction comparison across step counts and perturbation ratios (Table 4).

The key empirical insight that very few inversion steps (S=3) suffice—and that reconstruction-based baselines require burdensome timestep/step-count tuning while inversion is tuning-free—is well supported by Table 4 and the scoring ablation in Table 13.

The method is inference-stage only and plug-and-play, demonstrated by consistent FPS gains when inserted into other diffusion AD models (Table 5), which increases its practical usefulness. Implementation details, hyperparameters, and hardware are reported in detail, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The claim of 'state-of-the-art AD performance' is overstated at the pixel level: on MVTecAD multi-class, pixel AP (46.5 vs 52.6) and AU-PRO (92.7 vs 93.2) trail OmiAD, and mAD (83.7) is below OmiAD (85.3). The headline contribution is primarily image-level accuracy plus efficiency; the abstract/intro should be more precise about this.

Novelty is moderate: the core idea of measuring typicality via the PF-ODE trajectory/score norm for out-of-distribution detection already exists (Heng et al. 2024, ScoreDD, Osada et al. 2023), and DDIM inversion is standard. The contribution is essentially adapting these to latent-space AD with very few Euler steps, plus a heuristic scoring rule. The paper acknowledges these sources but the framing as a fundamentally new paradigm somewhat oversells the delta.

The most striking result—that inversion performance *degrades* with more accurate inversion (99.0 at S=3 vs 95.4 at S=1000 in Table 4)—is counterintuitive and not well explained theoretically. If the paradigm truly relies on PF-ODE determinism and one-to-one mapping to the prior, better Euler approximation should not hurt. This suggests the method may be exploiting coarse-inversion artifacts rather than the stated density argument, which deserves deeper analysis.

The anomaly scoring is heuristic: Algorithm 1 line 15 combines abs(max-min) of the channel norm with an unweighted sum over the map, and the pixel-level map is simply an upsampled low-resolution norm map, which likely explains the weaker localization metrics. The rationale is plausible but the design feels ad hoc.

Fairness of some comparisons is questionable: the headline model is a 1223M-parameter DiT-gigant plus EfficientNet-B4 encoder, and Table 7 shows much lighter variants (MLP, 351M) reaching 241 FPS with 97.2 AU-ROC; the paper does not compare against EfficientAD (cited as >200 FPS) or other strong non-diffusion methods in the main tables, so the efficiency/accuracy trade-off versus the broader field is not fully characterized.

Ablation on feature-space choice (Table 6) shows a large drop with weaker encoders (87.1 AU-ROC with VAE vs 99.0 with EfficientNet), indicating heavy dependence on the pretrained backbone rather than the diffusion modeling itself—consistent with prior work but weakening the paradigm-level claim.

Presentation has multiple typos and rough edges ('depiciton', 'uncertainly', 'image-lavel', 'acclerate compuatation', odd Figure 1 caption 'paradigm. and Conventional'), and code/project links are placeholders, which limits immediate reproducibility despite detailed documentation.
